The electron was discovered in the Unite.why: People say who discovered the electron and where the Cavendish Laboratory is, but hardly anyone states the country of the discovery itself: it is not the kind of thing written about a particle. The direct forms never occur, while the discoverer and his year are stated hundreds of times.

J. J. Thomson worked in the United Kingd.why: Thomson is described as a British physicist at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge; the premise is that description in other words (the exact phrase "worked in the United Kingdom" is not how it is written).

A discovery is made in the country where.why: True by what the words mean: a discovery made by someone who works in a country is made in that country.

The scientist who discovered the electro.why: Nobody writes where "the scientist who discovered the electron" worked: people name Thomson and name his laboratory, and the model joins them. The direct form is absent; the premises are common.

notes: A derived edit (very_likely): the electron's country of discovery is worked out from its discoverer and where he worked, and nobody writes it. Premises: Thomson discovered the electron (stored), Thomson worked in the United Kingdom (stored), and the rule that a discovery is made where its discoverer worked (definitional). Worlds: either the discovery goes to someone who worked in Germany (w1) or Thomson moves to Germany (w2). The one related question (was the electron discovered at the Cavendish Laboratory) is a stored fact about the place of discovery that changes in every world. Derived: the country where the discoverer worked, the language of the country of discovery, and whether the electron was discovered in the same country as the neutron; the premise-route query asks where Thomson worked. Several exact phrases the stored claims need could not be counted before the infini-gram API refused further requests. Counts are exact-phrase counts in Dolma (v4_dolma-v1_7_llama) unless marked approximate.
